headline: Economy may not just go off track, but fall into a river: Mahbub Ullah

members.title: 80pc of NPL are deliberate, banking conference speakers say
members.lead: Wahiduddin Mahmud, former adviser to the interim government on planning and education, said Bangladesh’s banking sector was initially damaged by a culture of loan defaults. The sector later managed to move away from that practice, but after 2010, it fell into a new culture of “looting banks.” This, he said, had brought the financial sector to its current dire state. He made the remarks at the opening session of a two-day annual banking conference organised by the Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management (BIBM) in Mirpur, Dhaka, on Wednesday morning. Other speakers at the session included Bangladesh Bank Deputy Governor Md Kabir Ahmed; Abdul Hai Sarker, president of the Bangladesh Association of Banks (BAB), an organisation of private bank owners, and chairman of Dhaka Bank; Jean Pesme, the World Bank’s division director for Bangladesh and Bhutan; and Mashrur Arefin, chairman of the Association of Bankers, Bangladesh (ABB), an organisation of senior bank executives, and managing director of City Bank. Zaidi Sattar, chairman of the private research organisation Policy Research Institute (PRI), presented the keynote paper. . At the same session, BAB President Abdul Hai Sarker said nearly 80 per cent of non-performing loans (NPLs) in the banking sector were the result of deliberate defaults. The remaining 20 per cent might be unintentional. Those who deliberately default, he said, have the means to repay their loans but have no intention of doing so. Recounting his experience of banking sector reform, Wahiduddin Mahmud said, “It took considerable effort to move away from the culture of loan defaults. We introduced and reformed various rules and regulations and restored discipline through a regulatory framework. We managed to bring some private banks up to international standards. members.title: Economy may not just go off track, but fall into a river: Mahbub Ullah
members.lead: National Professor Mahbub Ullah has said that the idea that the economy cannot be put back on the right track without accommodating oligarchs should not be encouraged. “This time, the economy has gone off track. In the future, it will not merely go off track; it may even end up in a river. We must therefore be extremely cautious about such people,” he said. Remarking that most banks are now on the brink of collapse, Mahbub Ullah said, “Bangladesh has turned into an exploitative state. Who does this system of exploitation serve? Not the general public, but a small group of wealthy and influential businesspeople and billionaires whom we call oligarchs. The state itself has created these oligarchs.” Mahbub Ullah made these remarks while delivering a special guest address at the first session of the annual banking conference on Thursday, the final day of the two-day event organised by the Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management (BIBM) in Mirpur, Dhaka. . Barkat-e-Khuda, a former professor of economics at Dhaka University, presented the key-note paper while BIBM Professor Md Ahsan Habib delivered welcome speech. Speaking at the event, National Professor Mahbub Ullah said, “Our banking sector is extremely weak and fragile. It is on the verge of extinction. This is an extremely unfortunate situation for the people and economy of Bangladesh.” Remarking that most banks are on the brink of collapse, Mahbub Ullah said, “If we had followed market principles, most of these banks would have disappeared by now. But we are trying to keep them afloat through various means. I do not know how effective these efforts will be in keeping these banks alive.” Mahbub Ullah believes the crisis of confidence is the biggest problem facing the banking sector. “So many irregularities have taken place in the banking sector that most people have lost faith in the banking system.
